elements.char: Homologous pairing of DNA molecules is involved in many fundamental biological processes,
elements.label: text

elements.char: including homologous recombination in meiosis, interaction between alleles on homologous
elements.label: text

elements.char: chromosomes (transvection) [1], and homologous repair of double strand breaks [2]. Recent
elements.label: text

elements.char: experiments have shown that dsDNA fragments in solution are capable of pairing in a homol-
elements.label: text

elements.char: ogy-dependent manner even in the absence of proteins [2–8]. This protein-free mode of pair-
elements.label: text

elements.char: ing, which can also occur in the presence of nucleosomes [7], is robust to salt concentration,
elements.label: text

elements.char: PH, and shear force, suggesting that it may serve as the ‘default’ mode of chromosome pairing
elements.label: text

elements.char: in vivo

elements.char: [2]. Various models have been proposed to explain the homology-dependent attraction
elements.label: text

elements.char: between dsDNA molecules [9–11], many of which attribute this interaction to hydrophobic
elements.label: text

elements.char: forces or electrostatics. Molecular dynamics simulations [11] show that adsorbed positive ions
elements.label: text

elements.char: lie in the grooves of DNA molecules, which may suggest an attractive dipole-dipole attraction.
elements.label: text

elements.label: text

elements.char: ing process have not been studied.

elements.char: The homologous pairing of dsDNA molecules is one example of a biological system in
elements.label: text

elements.char: which two molecules spontaneously attach to each other as a result of attractive interactions
elements.label: text

elements.char: between multiple matching binding sites. Other
elements.label: text

elements.char: in vivo
elements.label: text

elements.label: text

elements.char: DNA or RNA binding by proteins, target binding by small regulatory RNAs, and gene editing
elements.label: text

elements.char: by CRISPR/Cas9. Such pairing processes face at least three key demands. First, they must form
elements.label: text

elements.char: a product within a biologically reasonable timescale (speed). Second, they must form a product
elements.label: text

elements.char: that is durable enough to perform a subsequent function (stability). Third, the error rate must
elements.label: text

elements.char: be acceptably low for the given system (stringency) [12]. However, in systems where recogni-
elements.label: text

elements.char: tion involves many binding sites that contribute collectively to the interaction, the tradeoff
elements.label: text

elements.char: between parameters can be incompatible with system requirements. This incompatibility has
elements.label: text

elements.char: been referred to as the speed-stability-stringency (SSS) paradox [12–17].
elements.label: text

elements.char: Previously it has been shown that the tradeoff between speed and stability can be mitigated
elements.label: text

elements.char: if the testing process is divided into multiple steps, characterized by different binding energies
elements.label: text

elements.char: [14, 15]. Additionally, mechanisms of kinetic proofreading can allow such systems to achieve
elements.label: text

elements.char: arbitrarily good stringencies [18, 19], at the expense of searching speed. In general, the tradeoff
elements.label: text

elements.char: between speed, stability, and stringency depends strongly on the environment in which the
elements.label: text

elements.char: search is performed, which includes the prevalence of near matches in the sample being
elements.label: text

elements.char: searched, and the average time between collisions. The effectiveness of search strategies is also
elements.label: text

elements.char: influenced by specific details of the interaction, such as the binding energies of matching sites
elements.label: text

elements.char: and the characteristic decay length of the binding interaction.

elements.char: Here, we investigate how a feature that is intrinsic to any collision between DNA duplexes–
elements.label: text

elements.char: their freedom to rotate following a collision–affects the dynamics of homologous pairing. The
elements.label: text

elements.char: rotational degree of freedom provides a continuum of testing stages characterized by different
elements.label: text

elements.char: effective binding energies and interaction times. By analyzing an effective tractable model, we
elements.label: text

elements.char: show that the rotational degree of freedom mitigates tradeoffs between speed, stability, and
elements.label: text

elements.char: stringency as compared to a system in which the duplexes are rotationally constrained so that
elements.label: text

elements.char: they remain aligned. This new result provides insight into dynamics of dsDNA-dsDNA pair-
